new_statements.quote: [p. 69] Maring is a tonal language. Every change in tone can bring about a change in the meaning of a word. [...] In Maring there are three lexical tones. They are high (´), mid (-) and low (‘). [p. 73] All syllables have a nucleus and a tone. [...] In sesquisyllabic words, a stressed major syllable is preceded by a short unstressed C or CV minor syllable i.e., prefix C or CV + root CV or CVC (Haokip 2019:98; Lotven et al. 2020:15, 22). Usually, the vowel of the prefix is schwa. [p. 76] There are many limitations, as well as scope for further in-depth analysis of the prosodic features such as stress, intonation patterns etc, and in terms of sound change and variation, which the author hopes to carry out in the future.
new_statements.citation: Kanshouwa, Susie. 2025. A Phonological Sketch of Maring. Himalayan Linguistics 24(2): 62-77. DOI 10.5070/H9.35233 (eScholarship item 5pm0s5gr; CC BY-NC 4.0).
new_statements.locator: §4.3 Tone, p. 69 (tonemic chart Table 16, p. 70); §5.1.6 Phonotactic constraints, constraint 1, p. 73; §6.1 Schwa deletion, p. 73; §7 Summary and conclusion, p. 76
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Maring is a tone language: every syllable carries one of three lexical tones (high, mid, low), and tone, not stress, is the contrastive word prosody. The only statement about stress is structural: in sesquisyllabic words (schwa-prefix minor syllable + root), the root/major syllable is stressed and the preceding C/CV minor syllable is unstressed (so prominence falls on the root, i.e. the last syllable of such words); the unstressed schwa then deletes in fast speech, yielding clusters (kə+war > kwar 'bright', tʰə+luŋ > tʰluŋ 'stone'). No rule is given for stress in disyllabic compounds, and the author explicitly leaves stress and intonation for future work.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The stress remark is framed generally (with reference to Kuki-Chin literature: Haokip 2019, Lotven et al. 2020) rather than from a dedicated analysis; the conclusion says stress and intonation remain to be analysed. Tone description is 'surface level' only; earlier work (Ningomba 1978) recognised only two tones (falling, rising).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (word-list data from a native speaker of Machi village, Tengnoupal district). Sesquisyllabic words = prefix + monosyllabic root; morphemes are 'usually monosyllabic', longer words are compounds. Phrase-level tonal behaviour explicitly not covered.
new_statements.identity_note: Kanshouwa 2025 describes the variety of Machi village (Tengnoupal district), one of the 'standard' (non-Khoibu, non-Ramyangnga) Maring varieties; the paper's footnote cites Glottolog 'mari1415' but this is evidently a slip for mari1416 (Maring Naga). Ningomba 1978 describes standard Maring with dialect comparison across Lampiya (Lamlong Khunou), Lamlong Khulen, Machi and Khoibu, and sets up only two tones (falling, rising) versus Kanshouwa's three. Khoibu/Uipo (a sister variety treated as a separate language in Glottolog) is covered by Laishram 2015 and Saebo 2020/2021, not by the sources read here.

sources.note: Tonal language with three lexical tones (high, mid, low) on every syllable (p. 69, 73); in sesquisyllabic words the major (root) syllable is stressed and the schwa-prefix minor syllable is unstressed and deletes in fast speech (p. 73); stress and intonation explicitly deferred to future work (p. 76). Variety of Machi village.

sources.citation: Kanshouwa, Susie. 2024 (completed 2023). A dialectal study of Maring. Ph.D. thesis, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi (guide Pauthang Haokip). xv+472 pp. Shodhganga handle 10603/579050.
sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonological inventories (onsets, nuclei, codas, rhymes, syllable structure of Saibol, Narum, Khoibu, Machi, Waithou) and ch. 4 Historical phonology contain no statement on stress, accent or tone (zero hits in all chapters); the literature review (pp. 31-32) only reports that Ningomba 1978 'briefly discussed the sound system and tones', that Yumnam 1990 noted 'tonal differences' between Lamlong Khunou and Khoibu, and that there is 'a remarkable difference in intonation pattern' between them. Silent on word stress.
